paragraphs.title: Praise for God's Judgment and Protection of the Vulnerable

answers: For His wonderful things and faithful counsels
For giving riches to every nation
easy.explanation: Isaiah says, “thou hast done wonderful things; thy counsels of old are faithfulness and truth.”
easy.q: For what does the prophet praise the Lord?

answers: The city became a heap and the defenced city a ruin
They were moved to the mountain
easy.explanation: The Lord made “of a city an heap” and “of a defenced city a ruin.”
easy.q: What happened to the city and the defenced city?

easy.explanation: The Lord is called “a strength to the poor” and “a strength to the needy in his distress.”
easy.q: For whom has the Lord been a strength?

answers: They will glorify Him, and terrible nations will fear Him
They will build Him a palace
medium.explanation: The verse says, “the strong people glorify thee” and “the city of the terrible nations shall fear thee.”
medium.q: How will the strong people respond to the Lord's works?

answers: Because He gives people large cities
Because He protects the needy in distress
Because He makes the poor rulers
medium.explanation: The Lord is a refuge and a shadow for those facing distress and the attack of the terrible ones.
medium.q: Why is the Lord compared to a refuge from the storm and a shadow from the heat?

answers: A place of safety and protection
medium.explanation: A refuge is a place where someone is sheltered from danger, fitting the Lord's protection in verse 4.
medium.q: What does the word “refuge” mean in this passage?

answers: God judges the powerful but protects the vulnerable
The poor build cities while nations destroy them
The needy rule over the strong
challenge.explanation: The passage describes ruined cities and humbled nations while presenting God as a shelter for the poor and needy.
challenge.q: What central contrast appears in verses 1–5?

answers: The terrible ones cannot be defeated
God provides protection from the violence of the terrible ones
challenge.explanation: The Lord is a refuge from the storm and a shadow from the heat caused by the terrible ones.
challenge.q: What does the comparison with the storm and heat emphasize?

answers: It explains how the poor become terrible ones
It describes the silencing and humbling of the terrible ones
challenge.explanation: The Lord brings down the noise of strangers and lowers the branch, or power, of the terrible ones.
challenge.q: How does verse 5 continue the ideas of the earlier verses?

paragraphs.title: The Redemptive Banquet and the Removal of Veils and Death

answers: For the kings of Moab only
easy.explanation: The verse says that the Lord will make a feast “unto all people.”
easy.q: For whom does the Lord of hosts prepare the feast?

easy.explanation: The Lord will destroy “the face of the covering” and “the vail” spread over the nations.
easy.q: What will be destroyed or removed from the people?

answers: It will be swallowed up in victory
easy.explanation: Isaiah says, “He will swallow up death in victory.”

answers: It is intended for one city only
It takes place in a desert
medium.explanation: It is a feast of fat things, marrow, and well-refined wines, describing abundance and excellence.
medium.q: What characterizes the feast prepared by the Lord?

answers: The covering over the peoples and nations is removed
The nations are separated from one another
medium.explanation: The covering and vail symbolize what hides or burdens the peoples; the Lord removes them.
medium.q: What is the result of removing the covering and the vail?

medium.explanation: “Well refined” describes wine that has been purified and made excellent.
medium.q: What does “well refined” mean in the description of the wines?

answers: The feast represents abundance and joy for all peoples
The feast represents the destruction of the mountains
The feast is only for those who won a war
challenge.explanation: The feast prepared for all people presents abundance, fellowship, and joy as part of redemption.
challenge.q: What connection exists between the feast and redemption?

answers: The wiping away of tears and the removal of reproach
The increase of the terrible ones' power
challenge.explanation: The Lord will swallow up death, wipe away tears, and take away the rebuke of His people.
challenge.q: What accompanies the destruction of death?

answers: That redemption is limited to one nation
That the covering and its removal concern humanity as a whole
That the feast takes place only in many cities
challenge.explanation: The references to “all people” and “all nations” emphasize the universal scope of the passage.
challenge.q: What does the repeated emphasis on all people and all nations highlight?

answers: For their God and the Lord
easy.explanation: They say, “this is our God; we have waited for him” and “this is the Lord.”

easy.q: What do they declare that the Lord will do?

easy.explanation: They say, “we will be glad and rejoice in his salvation.”
easy.q: How do they respond to salvation?

answers: Recognition of the God for whom they waited
medium.explanation: The people recognize that the God before them is the one for whom they have waited.
medium.q: What does the statement “this is our God” express?

answers: The salvation received turns their hope into joy
Joy causes them to turn away
medium.explanation: After waiting for the Lord, they rejoice when His salvation comes.
medium.q: What is the relationship between waiting and rejoicing in the verse?

medium.explanation: The verse explains the meaning by pairing rejoicing with being glad in God's salvation.
medium.q: What does “rejoice” mean in this context?

answers: They move from waiting for salvation to rejoicing in it
They move from joy to fear
They move from wealth to poverty
challenge.explanation: At first they have waited for the Lord; afterward they are glad and rejoice in His salvation.
challenge.q: What changes in Israel's condition from the beginning to the end of the verse?

answers: To emphasize the identity of the One for whom they waited
To describe the number of nations
challenge.explanation: The repeated wording stresses that the very God and Lord for whom they waited has saved them.
challenge.q: Why does the verse repeat the identification of God as “this” God and “this” Lord?

answers: Gratitude and joy over God's saving work
challenge.explanation: Their declaration of salvation and their rejoicing express gratitude and faith in God's action.
challenge.q: What religious response is reflected in Israel's words?

paragraphs.title: The Humbling of Moab and Its Proud Strongholds

easy.explanation: The verse says, “Moab shall be trodden down under him.”
easy.q: Who will be trodden down under the Lord?

answers: Straw trodden down for the dunghill
easy.explanation: Moab is compared to straw being trodden down for the dunghill.
The fortress will be laid “to the ground, even to the dust.”
easy.q: How far will the fortress of Moab be brought down?

medium.explanation: The Lord will bring down Moab's pride together with the spoils of their hands.
medium.q: What will the Lord do to Moab's pride?

answers: The Lord's action in bringing Moab down
medium.explanation: The image of the Lord spreading His hands is connected with bringing down Moab's pride.
medium.q: What does the spreading of the Lord's hands signify in the passage?

medium.explanation: A fortress is a strong, defended place, fitting the description of Moab's high fortified walls.
medium.q: What does “fortress” mean in this passage?

answers: Moab's power and pride are broken
challenge.explanation: Moab is trodden down, its pride is brought low, and its fortified walls are reduced to dust.
challenge.q: What idea is shared by verses 10–12?

answers: The ease and completeness of Moab's humiliation
challenge.explanation: The image presents Moab as something powerless that is easily crushed underfoot.
challenge.q: What does the comparison to straw being trodden down emphasize?

answers: The pride and the fortresses are brought down together
challenge.explanation: The passage connects the bringing down of Moab's pride with the destruction of its high fortified walls.
challenge.q: How does the description of the fortress in verse 12 relate to the pride in verse 11?
